title: SpaceX Shares Plunge: Barron’s Calls Stock “Cheaper and Cheaper” Amid Investor Frenzy
body:
SpaceX’s privately‑held shares have continued to slide in recent months, prompting a fresh wave of optimism from Wall Street analysts who see the price decline as an opportunity rather than a warning sign. Morgan Stanley’s aerospace‑focused analyst Adam Jonas reiterated his bullish stance on the company in a new research note, arguing that the “cheaper and cheaper” valuation now on offer could unlock outsized upside for investors who gain exposure to the firm’s rapid‑growth launch business and its expanding satellite‑services portfolio. The commentary arrives at a time when defense contractors such as Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Kratos are also being highlighted by a Redburn analyst as beneficiaries of rising military spending on next‑generation weapons and cost‑effective space‑based capabilities.

Jonas’ assessment rests on several pillars. First, SpaceX’s launch cadence has reached unprecedented levels, with more than 100 missions flown in the past twelve months and a pipeline that includes high‑profile contracts for Starlink broadband, NASA crewed flights and a growing roster of commercial customers. The company’s reusable rocket technology, now standard across its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy fleet, has driven launch costs down dramatically, allowing SpaceX to undercut traditional providers such as United Launch Alliance on price while maintaining high reliability. Second, the analyst points to the burgeoning revenue stream from the Starlink constellation, which now serves millions of users worldwide and is projected to generate upwards of $30 billion in annual sales by the end of the decade. The combination of a robust launch business and a subscription‑based satellite service creates a diversified earnings base that can sustain growth even if any single segment slows.

The “cheaper” valuation, however, is not without its skeptics. Critics note that SpaceX remains a private company, and its share price is determined largely by secondary‑market transactions that can be influenced by liquidity constraints and investor sentiment rather than fundamentals. Moreover, the firm faces mounting regulatory scrutiny over its satellite megaconstellation, with concerns about orbital debris and spectrum allocation potentially curbing expansion. Jonas acknowledges these risks but argues that the market’s focus on short‑term headwinds has eclipsed the longer‑term strategic advantages that SpaceX enjoys, such as its vertical integration, in‑house engine production and a talent pool that continues to attract top engineers.

The Redburn analyst’s parallel outlook on defense giants adds another layer to the narrative. As the United States and allied nations pour funds into modernizing their arsenals—particularly in hypersonic weapons, electronic warfare and autonomous systems—companies that can deliver low‑cost, high‑performance space components stand to benefit. Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Kratos each have deep ties to the Department of Defense and are positioning themselves to supply launch services, satellite payloads and ground‑segment technologies that complement SpaceX’s capabilities. The analyst suggests that these firms could capture a share of the “spillover” demand generated by SpaceX’s aggressive pricing, especially in contracts where the military seeks to leverage commercial launch capacity to reduce procurement costs.

Investors are therefore watching a confluence of trends: a private launch titan whose share price appears increasingly discount‑priced, a defense sector poised for a spending surge, and a broader market shift toward commercial‑space solutions that blur the lines between civilian and military applications. While SpaceX’s valuation may appear “cheaper” today, the company’s ability to sustain its launch cadence, expand Starlink’s subscriber base and navigate regulatory challenges will determine whether the current discount translates into real upside.

Looking ahead, analysts expect the next 12‑18 months to be pivotal. If SpaceX can lock in additional large‑scale contracts—particularly with the Pentagon or international telecom operators—its cash flow could solidify, justifying a higher valuation. Simultaneously, the defense industry’s embrace of cost‑effective space assets could create partnership opportunities, further integrating SpaceX’s services into the military supply chain. In that scenario, the “cheaper” price tag may soon become a relic, and investors who entered at current levels could reap significant returns as the company cements its dominance across both commercial and defense space markets.
